blocks.text: A teacher asks, 'Have you finished the assignment?' with a rising tune, and the class knows it is a genuine yes-or-no question. The same words said with a falling tune can sound like a challenge. Intonation is not decoration. In Paper 3 it is a tested choice, and so is the one word you thump for emphasis.

blocks.markdown:
**Intonation** is the rise and fall of the voice across a stretch of speech. For this examination you need two tunes:

- **Falling tune** (↘) — the voice drops at the end. Use it for statements, commands, and *wh*-questions (*where, when, why, who, what, how*).
- **Rising tune** (↗) — the voice goes up at the end. Use it for yes/no questions and for items in a list that are not yet finished.

**Emphatic stress** is different. It is extra force on one word in a sentence to contrast it with something else. WAEC prints that word in CAPITAL LETTERS and asks which question the sentence would answer.

blocks.title: The emphatic-stress rule
blocks.text: The correct option is the question that keeps every unstressed word the same and replaces only the CAPITALISED word with a contrast. If Adaeze bought a NEW bag, the matching question is 'Did Adaeze buy an old bag?' — not 'Did Tunde buy a new bag?' That second question would have capitalised ADAEZE, not NEW.

rows: A wh-question; the information gap is already named
We bought rice, beans, and yam.
Unfinished items rise; the last item falls
blocks.caption: Choosing a tune from the type of utterance

blocks.title: Matching a capitalised sentence to its question
blocks.prompt: The given sentence is: 'The principal SANCTIONED the prefect.' Which question is it the appropriate answer to?

steps.text: Find the capitalised word: SANCTIONED. That is the information being contrasted.
Everything else in the sentence is given: it is the principal, and it is the prefect.
The matching question must doubt only the action: Did the principal praise the prefect? (or warn, or ignore — any contrast with sanctioned).
Reject 'Did the vice-principal sanction the prefect?' — that would require PRINCIPAL in capitals.
Reject 'Did the principal sanction the class captain?' — that would require PREFECT in capitals.
The sentence answers the question that replaces only SANCTIONED.

blocks.answer: Did the principal praise (or otherwise not sanction) the prefect? — only the capitalised idea is contrasted.

blocks.markdown:
### How emphasis changes meaning

Take the sentence *Tunde stole the money yesterday* and move the thump:

- **TUNDE** stole the money yesterday — not Chinedu.
- Tunde **STOLE** the money yesterday — he did not borrow it.
- Tunde stole **THE MONEY** yesterday — not the phone.
- Tunde stole the money **YESTERDAY** — not last week.

Each version is a different reply. That is why the paper asks you to match the capitalised sentence to one question among four that look almost the same.

blocks.title: WAEC Oral English tip
blocks.text: For tune questions, name the sentence type first: statement, command, wh-question, or yes/no. Statements, commands and wh-questions fall; yes/no questions rise. For emphatic stress, cover the capitalised word with your finger and check which option has changed only that word. If an option changes a different word, it is wrong even if it sounds clever.

points: Falling tune is for statements, commands and wh-questions.
Rising tune is for yes/no questions and unfinished list items.
Emphatic stress puts extra force on one word to mark a contrast.
WAEC prints that word in capitals; the matching question replaces only that word.
Moving the emphasis from Tunde to yesterday changes the meaning the speaker is insisting on.
